analysis.one_liner: Sets federal standards for HMOs: emergency care coverage, specialist access, and bans on paying doctors to limit care.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House subcommittee in 1996 without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have imposed a set of rules on managed care plans (HMOs and similar plans). It required plans to cover emergency room visits without prior approval, let patients keep seeing a specialist without repeated referrals, cover out-of-network specialists when the plan has none for a condition, and banned paying doctors bonuses for cutting back on medically necessary care. It also required plans to disclose financial arrangements that restrict care, provide translation services, meet minimum doctor-to-patient staffing, offer grievance procedures, and keep patient information confidential. Violations would carry federal civil money penalties.
analysis.who_benefits: People enrolled in managed care plans, who would gain enforceable rights to emergency care, specialist access, honest information about how their plan pays doctors, and a complaint process. The bill was aimed especially at low-income and minority enrollees, with translation requirements and service plans for medically underserved areas.

how_it_helps.text: Plans must cover emergency services without regard to prior authorization or whether the hospital is in the plan's network, using a 'prudent layperson' standard for what counts as an emergency.

Patients referred to a specialist could continue treatment without repeated pre-authorization, and plans must cover an outside specialist when the plan has none with knowledge of the patient's condition.

Plans are banned from paying physicians or physician groups any bonus to reduce or limit medically necessary services, and only a licensed health care practitioner — not a plan administrator — may decide what treatment is medically necessary.

Plans must disclose financial arrangements that restrict referrals or limit services, protect enrollee information as confidential, and HCFA must set up complaint and grievance procedures for enrollees.

Plans must provide translation resources where 5% or more of enrollees in an area belong to a single ethnic-minority group that speaks English as a second language, and must file service plans for medically underserved populations.
Plans must maintain at least one physician for every 2,000 enrollees, offer a choice of at least three providers in each category, and keep covered services geographically accessible.

analysis.who_pays: Managed care plans would bear the cost of meeting these requirements — wider coverage, more providers, translation staffing, disclosure, and penalties for violations — costs likely passed to enrollees and employers through premiums. The Health Care Financing Administration would shoulder new enforcement work.
analysis.who_pays_short: Managed care plans and their sponsors

drawbacks.text: Requiring plans to cover any out-of-network provider a patient chooses, with only a 'reasonable' deductible and copay, could raise premiums for all enrollees and erode the network discounts that keep managed care premiums lower than traditional insurance.

The bill leans on federal regulators: it gives the Secretary power to set penalty amounts and requires HCFA to build a grievance system within 90 days, a short timeline that skeptics could call unworkable.

The one-physician-per-2,000-enrollees minimum and mandatory provider choice could be difficult for plans operating in rural or provider-shortage areas, where the bill also demands service commitments to underserved populations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient protections address real, documented practices of 1990s managed care — emergency care denials, gatekeeping referrals, and bonuses tied to limiting care. The costs are real too: freer access to out-of-network care and minimum staffing rules would push premiums up, and the bill gives regulators little time to build enforcement. On balance it is a consumer-protection bill with a plausible price, whose main design weakness is vagueness ('reasonable' cost limits) rather than aim.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Commerce Committee and then to its Health and Environment Subcommittee in July 1996, and no committee or floor vote ever happened before the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Nydia Velázquez introduced the bill on June 27, 1996, with introductory remarks printed in the Congressional Record.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Commerce the day it was introduced.
On July 10, 1996, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, where it remained with no further action for the rest of the Congress.
The bill had the sponsor and 7 Democratic cosponsors — all Democrats — and never advanced past subcommittee referral before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Managed care plans were better off: no federal requirements on emergency coverage, specialist access, disclosure, or doctor bonuses ever took effect from this bill, and enrollees kept whatever rights state law and plan contracts gave them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Managed care plans, untouched by federal rules

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 27, 1996 and never reported the bill or scheduled a markup.

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and it sat in committees controlled by the Republican majority without action.

industries.industry: Managed care plans (HMOs and similar health plans)
industries.note: The bill would have forced plans to pay for emergency and out-of-network care, stop bonus payments tied to limiting care, disclose financial arrangements, and face civil money penalties. The industry's business model of gatekeeping and cost-containment ran directly against the protections enrollees would have gained.

industries.industry: Employers offering managed care coverage as a benefit
industries.note: Employers would likely have seen premium increases from expanded coverage mandates, but their employees would have gained enforceable protections; the bill also touches employer fringe benefits as a regulated subject.
